description_full: PCB Bancorp operates as the bank holding company for PCB Bank that provides various banking products and services to small and middle market businesses and individuals in the United States. The company offers demand, savings, money market, time deposits, and certificates of deposit; and remote deposit capture, courier deposit and positive pay services, zero balance accounts, and sweep accounts. It also provides real estate loans, including commercial and residential, small business administration (SBA), multifamily, business property, and construction loans; commercial and industrial loans, such as commercial term and lines of credit, and SBA commercial term, trade finance, home, and mortgage warehouse; consumer loans comprising residential mortgage and other consumer loans; and automobile loans, unsecured lines of credit, and term loans. In addition, the company offers access to account balances, online transfers, online bill payment, and electronic delivery of customer statements; and mobile banking solutions, including remote check deposit and mobile bill pay. Further, it provides automated teller machines; cash management, debit and credit card, and online and mobile banking; and banking by telephone, mail, personal appointment, debit cards, direct deposit, and cashier's checks, as well as treasury management, wire transfer, and automated clearing house services. It operates through full-service branches and loan production offices. The company was formerly known as Pacific City Financial Corporation and changed its name to PCB Bancorp in July 2019. PCB Bancorp was founded in 2003 and is headquartered in Los Angeles, California.

financial_summary: PCB Bancorp is a small-cap financial services business with a $421M market cap on $116M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 8% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $24M in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.71× cash conversion.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 26% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
